body.statement:
For every \(N\geq1\) and \(g\geq0\), the joint orientation frontier is finite, is nondecreasing in each argument, and satisfies
\[
 \vartheta_{N,g}\leq\min\{2^g,\tau_N\}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \vartheta_{N,g}=2^g\qquad\text{whenever }N\geq2g+1.
\]
For five available vertices the exact finite recurrence values are
\[
 (\vartheta_{5,g})_{g=0}^{6}=(1,2,4,6,8,12,24),
 \qquad
 \vartheta_{5,g}=24\quad(g\geq6).
\]
body.proof_tex:
For a fixed connected simple graph \(H\), choosing \(X_i\) from the factor indexed by \(\{i,j\}\) is the same as orienting that edge toward \(i\). Consequently \(c_H(r)\) is exactly the number of orientations of \(H\) with indegree vector \(r\). Only finitely many labeled simple graphs on at most \(N\) vertices and finitely many orientations of each graph occur, so the maximum defining \(\vartheta_{N,g}\) is finite. Enlarging \(N\) or \(g\) enlarges the feasible collection, proving monotonicity.

Fix a spanning tree \(S\) of \(H\), write \(b=|V(H)|\), and put \(h=g(H)\). There are
\[
 |E(H)\setminus E(S)|=|E(H)|-(b-1)=h
\]
non-tree edges. For a prescribed indegree vector \(r\), fix orientations of those \(h\) edges. There is at most one compatible orientation of \(S\): at a leaf of the current tree, the prescribed residual indegree forces the orientation of its unique remaining tree edge, after which that leaf may be deleted. Induction on the number of tree vertices proves uniqueness. Therefore
\[
 c_H(r)\leq 2^h\leq 2^g.
\tag{1}
\]
The fixed-edge completion proved in \(\mathrm{lem:tournament\mbox{-}score\mbox{-}fiber\mbox{-}ceiling}\) also gives \(c_H(r)\leq\tau_N\) whenever \(b\leq N\). Taking the maximum over \(H,r\) proves
\[
 \vartheta_{N,g}\leq\min\{2^g,\tau_N\}.
\tag{2}
\]

We next prove the exact maximality threshold. If \(g=0\), the included one-vertex graph gives \(\vartheta_{N,0}\geq1=2^0\), which combines with (1); because \(N\geq1=2g+1\), the asserted equivalence holds. Now let \(g\geq1\). For sufficiency, form a bouquet of \(g\) triangles by taking a central vertex \(z\), two new vertices \(u_i,v_i\) for each \(1\leq i\leq g\), and the three edges
\[
 \{z,u_i\},\qquad \{u_i,v_i\},\qquad \{v_i,z\}
\]
for each \(i\). This connected simple graph has \(2g+1\) vertices, \(3g\) edges, and hence cyclomatic number
\[
 3g-(2g+1)+1=g.
\]
Orient each triangle as either of its two directed cycles. Every such choice has indegree \(g\) at \(z\) and indegree one at every \(u_i,v_i\). The choices are independent across triangles, so for
\[
 r_z=g,\qquad r_{u_i}=r_{v_i}=1
\]
the score fiber contains \(2^g\) orientations. Thus \(\vartheta_{N,g}\geq2^g\) when \(N\geq2g+1\), and (1) proves equality.

For necessity, suppose \(\vartheta_{N,g}=2^g\). Finiteness shows that some feasible connected simple graph \(H\) on \(b\leq N\) vertices and some \(r\) attain this maximum. If \(h=g(H)\), then (1) gives
\[
 2^g=c_H(r)\leq2^h\leq2^g,
\]
so \(h=g\), and all \(2^h\) orientations of the cotree \(E(H)\setminus E(S)\) extend to orientations in the score fiber: the restriction map from the score fiber to the \(2^h\) cotree orientations is injective by the tree-uniqueness argument and has equally large domain and codomain.

We make the resulting constraint explicit. Give every tree edge \(s\) ordered endpoints \((a_s,b_s)\), and let \(y_s=1\) mean that \(s\) is oriented toward \(b_s\), while \(y_s=0\) means that it is oriented toward \(a_s\). Similarly order the cotree edges \(f_j\), \(1\leq j\leq h\), and encode their orientations by \(x_j\in\{0,1\}\). Delete one vertex row from the oriented incidence matrix of \(S\), obtaining a square matrix \(Q\), and let \(C\) be the correspondingly reduced incidence matrix of the cotree. Since \(S\) is a tree, leaf elimination makes \(Q\) invertible. The prescribed-indegree equations have the form
\[
 Qy=\beta-Cx,
 \qquad
 y(x)=Q^{-1}\beta-Q^{-1}Cx
\tag{3}
\]
for a constant vector \(\beta\) determined by \(r\) and the chosen endpoint orders.

For the cotree edge \(f_j\), let \(P_j\) be the unique path in \(S\) joining its endpoints. The unique solution of the incidence equation for the \(j\)-th column of \(C\) is unit flow along \(P_j\); hence the \(j\)-th column of \(Q^{-1}C\) is zero off \(P_j\) and is \(1\) or \(-1\) on every edge of \(P_j\), with the sign determined by the endpoint orders. Consequently each coordinate in (3) is an affine function
\[
 y_s(x)=\alpha_s+\sum_{j:s\in P_j}\epsilon_{sj}x_j,
 \qquad \epsilon_{sj}\in\{-1,1\}.
\tag{4}
\]
Every \(x\in\{0,1\}^h\) extends, so \(y_s(x)\in\{0,1\}\) on the full Boolean cube. The range diameter of the affine function in (4) on that cube is
\[
 \max_x y_s(x)-\min_x y_s(x)
 =\sum_{j:s\in P_j}|\epsilon_{sj}|.
\tag{5}
\]
Its left side is at most one. Thus every tree edge belongs to at most one of \(P_1,\ldots,P_g\); these fundamental-cycle paths are pairwise edge-disjoint. Because \(H\) is simple and \(f_j\notin E(S)\), the path \(P_j\) cannot have length one, for that would make its unique tree edge parallel to \(f_j\). Therefore \(|P_j|\geq2\), and edge-disjointness gives
\[
 b-1=|E(S)|\geq\sum_{j=1}^{g}|P_j|\geq2g.
\]
Since \(b\leq N\), necessarily \(N\geq2g+1\). Together with the bouquet construction this proves
\[
 \vartheta_{N,g}=2^g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N\geq2g+1.
\tag{6}
\]

It remains to certify the five-vertex values. Given a labeled graph \(H\) with lexicographically ordered edges \(e_j=\{u_j,v_j\}\), define
\[
 A_{H,0}(r)=\mathbf 1\{r=0\},
 \qquad
 A_{H,j}(r)=A_{H,j-1}(r-\mathbf e_{u_j})
             +A_{H,j-1}(r-\mathbf e_{v_j}),
\tag{7}
\]
where a term with a negative coordinate is zero. Expanding one factor at a time proves by induction that
\[
 A_{H,|E(H)|}(r)=c_H(r).
\tag{8}
\]
Put \(\mu(H)=\max_r c_H(r)\), and let \(N_{b,m}(s)\) be the number of connected labeled graphs on \([b]\) with \(m\) edges and \(\mu(H)=s\). Applying the additions in (7) to every subset of the at most ten possible edges gives the following finite audit table; within a row, \(N(s)\) abbreviates \(N_{b,m}(s)\), and a blank entry is zero:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|l|c}
b&m&\{s:N_{b,m}(s)\ne0\}&\sum_sN_{b,m}(s)\\ \hline
1&0&N(1)=1&1\\
2&1&N(1)=1&1\\
3&2&N(1)=3&3\\
3&3&N(2)=1&1\\
4&3&N(1)=16&16\\
4&4&N(2)=15&15\\
4&5&N(3)=6&6\\
4&6&N(4)=1&1\\
5&4&N(1)=125&125\\
5&5&N(2)=222&222\\
5&6&N(3)=190,\ N(4)=15&205\\
5&7&N(4)=50,\ N(5)=60,\ N(6)=10&120\\
5&8&N(7)=15,\ N(8)=30&45\\
5&9&N(12)=10&10\\
5&10&N(24)=1&1
\end{array}
\tag{9}
\]
This table is independently checkable without graph-isomorphism choices: scan the edge subsets in lexicographic order, reject a subset unless a search from vertex \(1\) reaches all \(b\) vertices, and use (7). As an arithmetic checksum, if \(a_{b,m}=\sum_sN_{b,m}(s)\), decomposition by the connected component containing vertex \(1\) gives
\[
 a_{1,0}=1,
 \qquad
 a_{b,m}=\binom{\binom b2}{m}
 -\sum_{q=1}^{b-1}\binom{b-1}{q-1}
   \sum_{\ell=0}^{m}a_{q,\ell}
   \binom{\binom{b-q}{2}}{m-\ell}.
\tag{10}
\]
Substitution in (10) gives exactly the last column of (9).

The maxima in the seven five-vertex rows are attained explicitly. Let
\[
 S_0=\{12,13,14,15\},
\]
and, for \(0\leq h\leq6\), let \(H_h\) have edge set \(S_0\cup A_h\), where the following table also gives a score vector whose coefficient is maximal:
\[
\begin{array}{c|l|c|c}
h&A_h&r&c_{H_h}(r)\\ \hline
0&\varnothing&(4,0,0,0,0)&1\\
1&\{23\}&(3,1,1,0,0)&2\\
2&\{25,34\}&(2,1,1,1,1)&4\\
3&\{23,24,25\}&(2,2,1,1,1)&6\\
4&\{23,24,25,34\}&(2,2,2,1,1)&8\\
5&\{23,24,25,34,35\}&(2,2,2,2,1)&12\\
6&\{23,24,25,34,35,45\}&(2,2,2,2,2)&24
\end{array}
\tag{11}
\]
Each coefficient in (11) follows by the same recurrence (7), after the four star edges have been processed. Since a connected graph with \(b\) vertices and \(m\) edges has cyclomatic number \(m-b+1\), (9) supplies the upper bounds and (11) supplies matching lower bounds for every \(0\leq g\leq6\). Hence
\[
 (\vartheta_{5,g})_{g=0}^{6}=(1,2,4,6,8,12,24).
\]
Finally a simple graph on at most five vertices has cyclomatic number at most
\[
 \binom52-5+1=6.
\]
Thus increasing \(g\) beyond six adds no feasible graph, and \(\vartheta_{5,g}=24\) for every \(g\geq6\).
